tagline: Basketball nation with a baroque heart
overview:
Lithuania is the largest and southernmost of the three Baltic states, lying on the eastern shore of the Baltic Sea with Latvia to the north, Belarus to the east, and Poland and Russia's Kaliningrad region to the south. It is about the size of West Virginia, mostly flat, with forests, lakes, and farmland. The capital, Vilnius, has one of the largest and best-preserved baroque old towns in Europe, a maze of courtyards, church towers, and cobbled lanes.

Around 2.9 million people live in Lithuania and speak Lithuanian, one of the oldest living languages in Europe, so conservative that it still shares features with ancient Sanskrit. Most Lithuanians are Roman Catholic. The country is a parliamentary republic that regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1990, the first Soviet republic to do so, and it joined the European Union and NATO in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2015. Lithuania is a leader in lasers and technology, and its people are so devoted to basketball that it is called the country's second religion.
landAndNature: Lithuania is a land of glacial lowlands, with its highest point, Aukštojas Hill, at just 294 meters. About 3,000 lakes glitter in the east, and the Nemunas River winds across the country to a lagoon on the coast. The Curonian Spit, a 98-kilometer sandbar shared with Russia, has some of the highest drifting sand dunes in Europe, with pine forests on one side and the open Baltic on the other; it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Forests cover about a third of the country and hold wolves, lynx, moose, and European bison in the Panevėžys region. White storks are so common that Lithuania has the highest density of nesting storks in Europe, and the stork is the national bird. Winters are cold and snowy, summers mild.
peopleAndCulture: Lithuanians treasure their ancient language, folk songs called sutartinės, sung in overlapping rounds, and the tradition of wooden cross-crafting, both recognized by UNESCO. Cepelinai, huge potato dumplings shaped like zeppelins and stuffed with meat, are the national dish, along with cold pink beet soup, dark rye bread, and šakotis, a spiky tree-shaped cake baked on a rotating spit. Midsummer, Joninės, is celebrated with wreaths and bonfires, and Užgavėnės, before Lent, features masked parades and burning a straw effigy of winter. Basketball is a national passion: Lithuania has won the European championship three times and Olympic bronze several times, and its players star in the NBA. The Hill of Crosses near Šiauliai holds more than 100,000 crosses left by pilgrims.
history: Baltic tribes lived here for millennia, and in 1253 Mindaugas was crowned the first and only king of Lithuania. The Grand Duchy of Lithuania became one of the largest states in Europe in the 1400s, stretching from the Baltic to the Black Sea, and joined with Poland in 1569 to form a commonwealth. Lithuania was the last pagan country in Europe, converting to Christianity in 1387. The Russian Empire absorbed it in 1795. Independence was declared in 1918, but the Soviet Union occupied Lithuania in 1940, followed by Nazi Germany, which murdered most of the country's large Jewish population, and then Soviet rule again, with mass deportations to Siberia. On March 11, 1990 Lithuania became the first Soviet republic to declare independence; Soviet troops killed 14 civilians in Vilnius in January 1991 before withdrawing.
funFacts: Lithuanian is considered the most conservative living Indo-European language, and linguists study it to understand ancient tongues.
The Hill of Crosses holds more than 100,000 crosses; Soviet authorities bulldozed it three times, and people rebuilt it each time.
Lithuania claims the geographic center of Europe, marked by a monument north of Vilnius, based on a 1989 French calculation.
Lithuania makes about a tenth of the world's scientific lasers, and they are used in labs on every continent.
The Vilnius neighborhood of Užupis declared itself an independent republic on April Fools' Day 1997, with its own constitution and army of about a dozen.
